analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $20 an hour over four years and phases out subminimum wages for tipped, teen, and disabled workers.
analysis.headline: A single senator introduced the bill in February 2026; with no cosponsors and no committee action since referral, it has not moved.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the federal minimum wage in steps: $10 an hour three months after enactment, $13 after a year, $16.50 after two, and $20 after three. After that, the wage would rise each year by the larger of inflation or GDP growth. It also phases out the separate, lower minimum wages for tipped workers, teenagers in their first jobs, and workers with disabilities, bringing all of them to the full federal minimum within about six years. It was referred to the Senate labor committee and has not been taken up.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers earning less than $20 an hour, tipped workers who could keep all their tips and eventually earn the full minimum, workers with disabilities now paid under special certificates that allow below-minimum wages, and teenagers in entry-level jobs whose subminimum wage would be phased out.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $10 on the effective date, then $13 after one year, $16.50 after two, and $20 after three [S2].

After reaching $20, the wage is indexed annually to the greater of the Consumer Price Index increase or the GDP increase, so it keeps rising with the economy rather than stalling for decades as the current $7.25 has [S2].

Phases the tipped minimum wage up from $6 to $20 over six years, then repeals the separate tipped wage entirely, so tipped workers must be paid the full federal minimum and gain an explicit right to keep all tips [S2].

Phases out the special certificates that allow employers to pay workers with disabilities less than the minimum wage, raising those rates to $20 over six years and then sunsetting the certificates, with Labor Department transition assistance for affected employers and workers [S2].
Phases out the $4.25 youth subminimum wage for newly hired workers under 20, stepping it up until it reaches the full minimum [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay low wages — restaurants, retail, fast food, agriculture, and other small businesses — would face higher labor costs, likely passed partly to consumers in prices; employers holding disability wage certificates would lose a below-minimum-wage workforce they have relied on.

drawbacks.text: Employers in low-wage industries would face substantial cost increases, and opponents of minimum wage increases generally argue some employers respond by raising prices, cutting hours, or hiring fewer workers [S2].

Indexing the wage to the greater of inflation or GDP growth is unusual: GDP can grow faster than prices, so the wage could keep rising even in low-inflation years, outpacing what some employers and regions can absorb [S2].
A single national wage applies to very different local economies; the same $20 rate binds rural and high-cost areas alike, which is the standard objection to a uniform federal floor [S2].

Eliminating the disability subminimum would end a program some families and employers argue preserves work opportunities for people with severe disabilities, though the bill includes transition assistance and disability advocates have long pressed to end it [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the gains are large and concrete: a wage floor that nearly triples from $7.25 to $20 and can no longer sit unchanged for decades, plus an end to legal subminimum pay for tipped, teen, and disabled workers. The costs are real but contested: higher labor costs for low-wage employers, uncertain effects on hours and hiring, and a GDP-based index that could push the wage up faster than prices in some years. Whether job losses offset wage gains is a genuine empirical dispute, but the bill's design is coherent and its benefits flow directly to the lowest-paid workers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on February 4, 2026, and nothing has happened since.

narrative.text: Senator Ruben Gallego introduced S. 3780 in the Senate on February 4, 2026 [S1][S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day; that is the entire action history [S4].
No senators have cosponsored the bill — zero from either party [S3].
The 119th Congress is still in session, so the bill remains alive in committee but has not advanced [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has moved; employers paying low or subminimum wages are unaffected while the bill sits without cosponsors or committee action.

for.name: Sen. Ruben Gallego
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to the Senate HELP Committee

sides.party_line_note: There has been no vote and no debate; no senator of either party has cosponsored the bill, so the partisan shape of support is not yet on the record [S3].

industries.note: The bill would phase out the tipped minimum wage entirely after six years, requiring restaurants to pay servers the full $20 federal minimum plus any tips they keep. Servers' pay rises, but the industry's ability to pay a lower cash wage disappears.

industries.industry: Retail, fast food, and other low-wage employers
industries.note: A $20 national floor would directly raise payroll costs for the largest employers of minimum-wage workers, likely pushing some of it to consumers in prices.

industries.industry: Employers holding disability subminimum-wage certificates (sheltered workshops and disability employment agencies)
industries.note: The bill ends new special certificates immediately and sunsets existing ones after the phase-in, removing the legal basis for paying workers with disabilities below the minimum wage.
The youth subminimum phase-out removes a cheaper first-90-days wage for teen hires, though the lower rate was small ($4.25) and short-lived.

analysis.trajectory: Minimum wage bills introduced by a single senator with zero cosponsors almost never reach a committee vote, let alone the floor, in a divided Congress where the majority has not embraced the proposal. Barring new cosponsors or a change in Senate leadership priorities, this bill is likely to die quietly at the end of the 119th Congress without a hearing or vote.
